patient_information: A 22-year-old male farmer from rural northern Ethiopia who had been in excellent health prior to the onset of his illness.
chief_complaint: Difficulty walking, which started 10 years prior to presentation.
history_of_present_illness: Ten years ago, the patient woke from sleep and noticed weakness in both legs. There was no history of trauma or prodromal symptoms. The weakness rapidly progressed over 4 to 5 days, resulting in the need for a cane for mobility. He reported no back pain, sensory complaints, sphincter disturbance, or upper limb symptoms. His walking difficulty has been stable and non-progressive since the initial onset.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is a farmer from rural northern Ethiopia. The onset of his illness coincided with a period of drought and famine, during which his diet consisted almost exclusively of grass peas (Lathyrus sativus, local name guaya). He was engaged in hard physical labor on his family farm. During that time, several similar cases of weakness occurred among young male farmers in his village. There was no history of cassava exposure in the region.
physical_exam: The patient is an alert young man with a normal mental state. His gait is spastic ('scissor gait'), with foot-dragging and toe-scraping. Examination reveals mild bilateral lower limb spastic weakness of a pyramidal pattern, with pathologically brisk deep tendon reflexes and sustained foot clonus. An extensor plantar response is present on the right and equivocal on the left. Cranial nerves and upper limbs are normal, and there is no sensory or bladder dysfunction.
labs_and_diagnostics: Full blood count, liver function tests, renal function tests, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, nerve conduction studies, and electromyography were all normal. HIV-1 serology was non-reactive. HTLV-1 and -2 serology and MRI were not available.
differential_diagnosis: The clinical syndrome is an upper motor neuron lesion with spastic paraparesis. Compressive, hereditary, infectious, and metabolic myelopathies were considered less likely due to the absence of radicular symptoms, sensory level, or back pain, as well as the non-progressive course. HTLV-associated myelopathy (HAM) was deemed unlikely due to its typical insidious onset and prominent sensory and bladder symptoms. Neurocassavism (konzo) was ruled out by the lack of cassava exposure. A diagnosis of neurolathyrism was favored based on male gender, physical exertion, and excessive consumption of guaya in an epidemic context.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient received physiotherapy and muscle relaxants, which resulted in only mild and short-lasting improvement of his spasticity. A walking cane and wheelchair were provided for mobility. He was counseled to avoid any further consumption of Lathyrus sativus.
final_diagnosis: The diagnosis is neurolathyrism, a preventable toxic myelopathy. This is based on the characteristic clinical presentation of irreversible, acute-onset spastic paraparesis without sensory or bladder involvement. The diagnosis is confirmed by the history of excessive and prolonged ingestion of the grass pea Lathyrus sativus, which contains the neurotoxin β-ODAP, during a period of famine. Supporting factors include his demographic (young male farmer), engagement in hard physical labor, and the epidemiological context of similar cases in his village.
